title: Hub GCSE History Topic Checklist (Aligned to Edexcel 1HI0)
subtitle: Option 10: Crime and punishment in Britain, c1000–present and Whitechapel, c1870–c1900: crime, policing and the inner city

exam_structure.paper_name: Paper 1: Thematic Study and Historic Environment
exam_structure.overview: Section A tests the Historic Environment site (16 marks, 25 mins). Section B tests the Thematic Study across 4 eras (36 marks, 55 mins) plus 4 marks for SPaG.

sections.title: c1000–c1500: Crime and punishment in medieval England

topics.title: 1. Nature and changing definitions of criminal activity
points: Crimes against the person, property & authority (incl. poaching as ‘social’ crime)
Shifting crime definitions after Norman Conquest (incl. William I’s Forest Laws)

topics.title: 2. The nature of law enforcement and punishment
points: Authorities & local communities in law enforcement in Anglo-Saxon, Norman & later medieval England (incl. tithings, the hue & cry & the parish constable)
Emphasis on deterrence & retribution, the use of fines, corporal & capital punishment; use & end of the Saxon Wergild

topics.title: 3. Case study
points: Influence of the Church on crime & punishment in the early thirteenth century: Sanctuary & Benefit of Clergy; the use of trial by ordeal & why it ended

sections.title: c1500–c1700: Crime and punishment in early modern England

topics.title: 1. Nature and changing definitions of criminal activity
points: Continuity & change: the nature of crimes against the person, property & authority (incl. heresy & treason)
New definitions of crime in the sixteenth century: vagabondage & witchcraft

topics.title: 2. The nature of law enforcement and punishment
points: Authorities & local communities in law enforcement (incl. town watchmen)
Continued use of corporal & capital punishment; introducing transportation & start of the Bloody Code

topics.title: 3. Case studies
points: The Gunpowder Plotters, 1605: their crimes & punishment
Case study — Matthew Hopkins & the witch-hunts of 1645–47; reasons for their intensity; the punishment of those convicted

sections.title: c1700–c1900: Crime and punishment in eighteenth- and nineteenth-

topics.title: 1. Nature and changing definitions of criminal activity
points: Continuity & change: the nature of crimes against the person, property & authority (incl. highway robbery, poaching & smuggling)
Changing definitions of crime exemplified in the ending of witchcraft prosecutions & treatment of the Tolpuddle Martyrs

topics.title: 2. The nature of law enforcement and punishment
points: Authorities & local communities in law enforcement (incl. Fielding brothers); development of police forces & rise of CID
Changing views on the purpose of punishment; use & end of transportation, public execution & the Bloody Code; Prison reform (incl. John Howard & Elizabeth Fry)

topics.title: 3. Case studies
points: Pentonville prison in the mid nineteenth century: why it was built; the strengths & weaknesses of the separate system in operation
Case study — Robert Peel – his contribution to penal reform & to the development of the Metropolitan Police Force

sections.title: c1900–present: Crime and punishment in modern Britain

topics.title: 1. Nature and changing definitions of criminal activity
points: Continuity & change: the nature of crimes against the person, property & authority (incl. new forms of theft & smuggling)
Changing definitions of crime (incl. driving offences, race crimes & drug crimes)

topics.title: 2. The nature of law enforcement and punishment
points: Authorities & local communities in law enforcement (incl. Neighbourhood Watch); Changes within the police force: increasing specialisation, use of science & technology & the move towards prevention
Abolition of the death penalty; changes to prisons (incl. open prisons & specialised treatment of young offenders); the development of non-custodial alternatives to prison

topics.title: 3. Case studies
points: Treatment of Conscientious Objectors in the First & Second World Wars
The Derek Bentley case: its significance for the abolition of the death penalty

sections.title: c1870–c1900: crime, policing and the inner city

topics.title: 2. Knowledge, selection and use of sources for historical enquiries
points: National & regional context: the working of the Metropolitan Police, the quality of police recruits; development of CID, Home Secretary & of Sir Charles Warren, public attitudes towards the police
Local source types: housing & employment records, council records & census returns, Charles Booth’s survey, workhouse records, local police records, coroners’ reports, photographs & London newspapers
National source types: national newspapers, records of crimes & police investigations, Old Bailey records of trials & Punch cartoons
Evaluating source strengths & limitations for historical enquiries
Formulating targeted follow-up questions for historical enquiries
Selecting relevant archival sources for follow-up investigations

sections.title: Historic Environment: Whitechapel, c1870–c1900: crime, policing and the inner city

topics.title: 1. Whitechapel, c1870–c1900: crime, policing and the inner city
points: Local context of Whitechapel; problems of housing & overcrowding; Attempts to improve housing: the Peabody Estate; Provision for the poor in the Whitechapel workhouses; Links between the environment & crime; Life in Whitechapel as an inner city area of poverty & discontent

Inhabitants of Whitechapel; lack of employment opportunities & level of poverty; prevalence of lodging houses & pubs creating a fluctuating population without ties to the community; impact of changing patterns of migration: the settlement of migrants from Ireland & Eastern Europe & the increase in Jewish migration during the 1880s

Organisation of policing in Whitechapel; ‘beat constable’; work of H division & the difficulties of policing the slum area of Whitechapel, the rookeries, alleys & courts; Problems of policing caused by crime & antisocial behaviour: alcohol, prostitution, protection rackets, gangs, violent demonstrations & attacks on Jewish people

Investigative policing in Whitechapel: developments in techniques of detective investigation (incl. sketches, photographs & interviews); problems caused by the need for cooperation between the Metropolitan Police, the City of London Police & Scotland Yard; Dealing with the crimes of Jack the Ripper & the added problems caused by the media reporting of the ‘Ripper’ murders; The Whitechapel Vigilance Committee
National & regional context: the working of the Metropolitan Police, the quality of police recruits; development of CID, Home Secretary & of Sir Charles Warren, public attitudes towards the police

topics.title: 2. Knowledge, selection and use of sources for historical enquiries
points: Local source types: housing & employment records, council records & census returns, Charles Booth’s survey, workhouse records, local police records, coroners’ reports, photographs & London newspapers
National source types: national newspapers, records of crimes & police investigations, Old Bailey records of trials & Punch cartoons

Formulating targeted follow-up questions for historical enquiries
Selecting relevant archival sources for follow-up investigations
